lesson.title: Test Functions: Proof Instead of 'It Looked Right'
lesson.summary: A test function calls your code with known inputs and checks the actual result against the expected result, and naming it test_something turns a one-time manual check into a permanent, repeatable, automatically discoverable proof that the code still works.
lesson.body:
You already know how to define a function, and you already have a general sense of what unit testing is trying to accomplish. A test function is simply an ordinary function, defined the same way as any other, whose entire job is narrower and more disciplined than a typical function's job: it calls the code under test with specific, known inputs, and then checks whether the result matches what you already know the correct answer should be, usually with an assert statement.

The naming convention matters more than it might first appear. By starting the function's name with test_, followed by a description of exactly what scenario it checks, you make the function discoverable, by yourself later, by teammates, and by testing tools like unittest or pytest that automatically scan a file for anything named that way and run it without you having to call each one by hand. This is the real difference between casually running your code once and eyeballing the output, and writing a genuine test function: the eyeball check happens once and is gone, but a test function stays in your project permanently, ready to be rerun automatically every single time you change the code, catching regressions where a change that fixed one thing silently broke another.

```python
def is_palindrome(text):
    cleaned = text.lower().replace(" ", "")
    return cleaned == cleaned[::-1]

def test_is_palindrome_true_for_simple_word():
    assert is_palindrome("level") == True

def test_is_palindrome_true_for_phrase_with_spaces():
    assert is_palindrome("race car") == True

def test_is_palindrome_false_for_non_palindrome():
    assert is_palindrome("python") == False

test_is_palindrome_true_for_simple_word()
test_is_palindrome_true_for_phrase_with_spaces()
test_is_palindrome_false_for_non_palindrome()
print("All tests passed")
```

is_palindrome("level") lowercases and strips spaces from "level", getting "level" back unchanged, and compares it to its own reverse, "level"[::-1], which is also "level", so it returns True. is_palindrome("race car") becomes "racecar" after removing the space, and "racecar" reversed is still "racecar", so it also returns True. is_palindrome("python") becomes "python", but reversed it is "nohtyp", which does not match, so it correctly returns False. Every assert inside every test function passes, none of them raise an AssertionError, so all three test function calls complete silently and the final print statement runs. The output is:

```
All tests passed
```

Each test function here checks exactly one scenario and its name says which one, that focus is deliberate. If test_is_palindrome_false_for_non_palindrome ever failed after some future change to is_palindrome, its name alone would tell you precisely what broke, without you needing to reread the whole function to figure out what it was even testing.
